Chapter 6: The Roots of Social Oppression—How Systems Shape the Individual.
Have you ever felt like the weight of the world is just a little heavier than it should be? It’s more than the usual stress, or those nagging self-doubts. There’s something bigger at play—something woven deep into the fabric of society itself.
You can sense it in the rules that don't quite make sense. In the expectations that seem impossible to meet. And in that subtle pressure—quiet, but always there—urging you to just keep your head down and stay in line.
That’s the reality of social oppression. These invisible forces shape our lives, often without us even noticing.
Imagine a young teacher, starting her very first year in the classroom, full of hope and eager to inspire her students. She’s got fresh ideas, a spark of creativity, and a real desire to make a difference. But pretty quickly, she runs into walls—standardized tests, rigid lesson plans, and all these unspoken rules about what’s “acceptable.”
Every time she tries to shake things up, she’s met with pushback. Not just from the folks in charge, but from other teachers, too. They warn her, “Don’t rock the boat.” Over time, that bright spark starts to fade. She learns to play by the rules, even when those rules don’t make much sense.
And it’s not just schools, is it? You see the same patterns in offices, in hospitals, in factories—even at home. Systems are built to keep things running smoothly, but sometimes they do it by stamping out individuality and fairness.
Most of us don’t realize just how much these structures guide our choices, shape our opportunities, or even limit what we think is possible.
It’s tempting to point fingers at individuals for their struggles—to say, “Well, you just need to try harder,” or, “Change your mindset.” But here’s something important: the deck is often stacked against people, whether they realize it or not. Social systems reward those who blend in and punish those who speak up. They build hierarchies, keeping some folks on top and others stuck below. The rules aren’t truly fair, and the playing field is rarely level.
Picture this—a factory worker, dreaming of a better future for his kids. Every day, he puts in long hours for little pay, barely earning respect. He’s told he should be grateful just to have a job, that he should keep quiet and accept things as they are. The message is loud and clear: don’t question, don’t hope for more, don’t expect change.
After a while, these messages start to sink in. People begin to believe their struggles are their own fault. That maybe they deserve their spot in the hierarchy. They stop imagining a different life, stop fighting for justice, and stop believing that change is even possible.
But here’s the truth: social oppression isn’t set in stone. It’s the result of choices—choices made by those who hold power, by those who quietly go along, and by those who choose to look the other way. Real change is possible. But it starts with opening your eyes to the system, seeing it for what it is, and refusing to accept its limits.
Most people never get to that point. They adapt. They endure. They survive. But for those who do, the first step always looks the same: realizing that the world isn’t as it should be—and that you have the power to imagine something better.
